title: Service Braking and Brake Indications
summary: Learn the difference between normal service braking, deceleration and pressure indications.
objectives: Identify the roles of brake cylinder and brake pipe
Explain why pressure values are system-dependent

sections.heading: Service braking
sections.body: Service braking is the normal controlled reduction of train speed. In the training controller B1, B2 and B3 represent progressively greater requests. Smooth control relies on anticipating a stop and observing the resulting speed change.

sections.heading: Brake cylinder pressure
sections.body: On pneumatic friction-brake equipment, pressure delivered to a brake cylinder can produce mechanical braking force through the brake gear. The precise response and indicated scale vary by vehicle and brake design.

sections.heading: Brake pipe pressure
sections.body: In train air-brake systems that use a brake pipe, pressure can convey braking and release commands through the train. Its relation to cylinder pressure is not universally the same for every multiple-unit or blended-brake arrangement.

sections.heading: Reading the gauges
sections.body: Read the gauge label and units first, then interpret the trend alongside speed. Pressure is not itself a measure of stopping distance: speed, gradient, adhesion, load and brake characteristics also matter. Any numeric pressures shown in this teaching simulator are illustrative, not certified rolling-stock values.

reviewQuestions.question: Which detent is the strongest configured service-brake request?
reviewQuestions.explanation: B3 is the strongest of the three configured service-braking positions.

reviewQuestions.question: What does brake cylinder pressure describe where pneumatic brakes are fitted?
choices: Pressure associated with a brake actuator
reviewQuestions.explanation: Brake cylinder pressure relates to a pneumatic brake actuator.

reviewQuestions.question: Do all trains use the same brake pipe and cylinder pressure relationship?
reviewQuestions.explanation: Brake arrangements, including electro-pneumatic and blended systems, differ across rolling stock.
